References / Textile / 309

Printed flannel with chevrons

A surviving swatch of Varvara Stepanova’s geometric flannel print, made when constructivist artists turned to designing textiles for Soviet factories.

Source
Victoria and Albert Museum, T.213-2016
Creator
Varvara Stepanova
Made
1924 (V&A)
Style
Constructivism (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Geometric, industrial, rhythmic
Evidence
Viewed the V&A photograph of the swatch T.213-2016 (1600 × 1443 px through the museum’s IIIF service) in a scratch folder. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A describes the swatch as printed cotton flannel, about 22 × 23–25 cm, “with geometric design of wine red and dull olive-brown chevrons on a pale fawn natural colour ground”, made in Russia in 1924. V&A.

After an official appeal in 1923, Stepanova, Popova, and Rodchenko designed prints for the Soviet textile industry. The V&A notes that rural buyers preferred floral prints, so surviving samples are rare. Stepanova’s grandson Alexander Lavrentiev gave the swatch to the V&A director Martin Roth in 2014. V&A.

Observed

  • Rows of chevrons point alternately up and down, in a wine red and an olive green-brown.
  • Pale bands of the unprinted ground run on two diagonals between the chevrons, so the pattern reads as a lattice of zigzags.
  • The edges are cut and slightly frayed; the flannel nap softens the edges of the print.

Why it belongs

The swatch shows the style’s diagonal energy transferred to an all-over repeat. The color is quieter than in the posters, which suggests that the red-and-black rule belongs to print, not to every constructivist medium.

Compare Popova’s design with stars in circles, which keeps red and black.

Borrow

Build a background pattern from two interlocking chevrons and let the gaps between them form a diagonal lattice.

Use a muted red with an earthy second color for a quieter version of the style.
